claims.text: The as-deposited protective coating has an FCC/BCC dual-phase microstructure.
The coating is FeNiCoCrMoAl-based.
The coating is susceptible to progressive plastic deformation at elevated temperature.
Creep resistance is primarily governed by the cooperative effects of dynamically formed nanoscale boundary precipitates and partial recrystallization.
Dynamic precipitates form at grain and phase boundaries during creep.
Local recrystallized domains develop within the FCC/BCC matrix during creep.
Boundary precipitates and recrystallized regions act as barriers to dislocation climb and glide.
The impediment of dislocation motion reduces the steady-state creep rate.
The proposed precipitate and recrystallization mechanism elevates the stress exponent.
Applied stress and temperature can alter the active creep mechanism and creep resistance.
In-situ TEM creep tests will vary stress from 50% of yield to near yield and temperature from 500 to 800 °C over periods of at least 10 hours.
Using an inert atmosphere or vacuum will limit oxidation and isolate intrinsic creep mechanisms.
A doped or phase-stabilized coating will have a lower steady-state creep strain rate than an otherwise identical undoped or unstabilized coating.
A doped or phase-stabilized coating will have a higher stress exponent than the baseline coating.
The baseline coating has fewer boundary precipitates, less dynamic recrystallization, and a faster creep rate.
The proposed mechanism remains significant at temperatures up to approximately 800 °C.
Above approximately 800 °C, precipitate coarsening or thermally activated softening reduces the mechanism's effectiveness.
The precipitate fraction or extent of boundary recrystallization required for optimal creep resistance is not quantified.
Small chemistry changes may alter the magnitude of creep resistance.
Failure to detect differences in creep rate or in dislocation pinning and precipitate evolution between modified and baseline coatings would fail to confirm the proposed synergy.

contradictions.description: The main intervention specifies only variation of stress and temperature, whereas the predicted comparison and falsification experiment require doped, phase-stabilized, or precipitate-stabilized coatings. No modifying chemistry or stabilization treatment is specified.
